qs.q: A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis has a genetic defect impairing Th17 cell differentiation. Why are these patients specifically susceptible to superficial Candida infections?
o: They lack mucosal secretory antibody responses
They cannot produce interferon for macrophages
They fail to recruit adequate tissue neutrophils
They suffer from impaired complement activation
qs.e: Th17 cells secrete IL-17, which is crucial for inducing epithelial antimicrobial peptides and recruiting neutrophils to mucosal surfaces.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

faq.a: Underlying Th17 deficiency impairs mucosal neutrophil recruitment, so fungi are not cleared even when drug levels are adequate.
faq.q: Why does CMC persist despite standard antifungal courses?

faq.a: No. Acute thrush is short‑lived and occurs in healthy hosts; CMC is chronic, relapsing, and signals immune dysfunction.
faq.q: Is CMC the same as acute thrush?

faq.a: Yes; isolated Th17 defects, HIV infection, and certain primary immunodeficiencies (e.g., Job syndrome) can produce CMC.

exam: What bedside clues would make you suspect an underlying immunodeficiency in a patient with chronic oral thrush? — Look for recurrent mucosal infections, family history of autoimmunity, and signs of endocrine failure.

How would you prioritize investigations for CMC in a district hospital lacking flow cytometry? — Perform KOH microscopy, culture if possible, and screen for HIV; treat empirically while arranging referral for immunology.

A patient on long‑term fluconazole develops liver enzyme elevation; what is your next step? — Switch to itraconazole or posaconazole if available; monitor liver function; consider topical therapy if systemic drugs are contraindicated.
Explain why azole resistance is more common in CMC than in acute candidiasis. — Chronic exposure selects for resistant strains; biofilm formation further reduces drug penetration.

In a teenager with CMC, hypocalcaemia and hyperpigmentation appear. What is the most likely diagnosis and next urgent action? — Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1; assess adrenal function and start stress‑dose steroids if Addison disease is suspected.

Distinguish CMC from cutaneous candidiasis secondary to diabetes. — CMC is chronic, involves multiple mucosal sites, and is linked to T‑cell defects; diabetic candidiasis is usually limited to intertriginous skin and improves with glucose control.
Why is systemic corticosteroid therapy contraindicated in uncontrolled CMC? — Steroids further suppress Th17 responses, worsening fungal overgrowth.

What infection control measures are needed for a patient with CMC in a ward? — Standard hand hygiene; no isolation needed as transmission is endogenous, but protect immunocompromised roommates from opportunistic infections.
ai.title: Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Persistent Candida infection of skin, nails and mucosa reflects T‑cell/Th17 defects, often linked to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and targeted immunology; treatment combines antifungals and immune modulation.

b: Key feature: infections last >3 months despite standard therapy
Often first sign of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS‑1)
Common in low‑resource settings where HIV, TB, malnutrition coexist
sections.p: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) is a group of disorders where Candida species cause persistent or recurrent infections of skin, nails, oral and genital mucosa. It is not a primary infection but a manifestation of underlying immune dysfunction, especially impaired Th17 immunity.

b: Germ‑tube test positive in C. albicans at 37 °C
Biofilm confers resistance to azoles and host defenses
sections.p: Candida albicans is the predominant species; other Candida (C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis) may be seen. Yeast forms germ‑tube production, hyphal transition and biofilm formation enable mucosal persistence.

b: Risk increased by antibiotics, steroids, diabetes, HIV
sections.p: Candida is a normal commensal of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. Overgrowth occurs when mucosal immunity is compromised. Person‑to‑person spread is rare; endogenous overgrowth is the rule.

b: Oral: white plaques that scrape off leaving erythema
Skin: macerated plaques in intertriginous zones
sections.p: Clinically CMC presents with chronic oral thrush, angular cheilitis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, onychomycosis and intertriginous dermatitis. In APS‑1 patients, endocrine failures (hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease) follow.
Diagnosis integrates clinical pattern, microscopy/culture and immune work‑up. In low‑resource hospitals, microscopy may be the only available test.

t.a: KOH wet mount of lesion scrapings
t.b: Confirms Candida hyphae; a positive result supports CMC when chronic lesions are present
Identifies species and antifungal susceptibility; if unavailable, treat empirically based on typical C. albicans pattern

t.a: Serum IgA, IgE and lymphocyte subset (CD4, Th17) counts
t.b: Detects T‑cell defects; low Th17 suggests APS‑1 or Job syndrome. If flow cytometry is unavailable, screen for APS‑1 with auto‑antibodies to IFN‑α/ω
Highly specific for APS‑1‑related CMC; not required for diagnosis but guides prognosis

b: Itraconazole or posaconazole for azole‑resistant isolates – limited availability
Topical clotrimazole or nystatin for localized lesions when systemic drugs not tolerated
Consider recombinant IFN‑γ or IL‑17 supplementation in research settings; not routine
Treat co‑existing HIV, diabetes or malnutrition to improve immunity
sections.p: Management targets the fungus, the immune defect and any associated endocrine disease. In low‑resource settings, oral fluconazole is first‑line; adjunctive immune therapy is considered when available.

b: Ask about family history of autoimmune disease – points to APS‑1
Check for other endocrine signs (hypocalcaemia symptoms, hyperpigmentation) – may coexist
In HIV‑positive patients, differentiate CMC from opportunistic esophageal candidiasis by chronicity and response to ART
sections.p: Focus on the immunological basis, the link with APS‑1, and pragmatic work‑up when advanced labs are missing.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid progression to extensive oral/esophageal ulceration causing dysphagia
Systemic signs: fever, hypotension, or sepsis from secondary bacterial infection
New onset adrenal crisis in a known APS‑1 patient
